A round church on the Caelian Hill in Rome, dedicated to Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr, whose body had been found in the Holy Land a few decades before. It was begun under Pope Leo I, with roof beams dated by their tree rings to about 455, and consecrated by Pope Simplicius between 468 and 483, probably paid for by the rich Valerii family whose estates covered the hill. It was the first church in Rome built on a round plan, and its design has no match in the late Roman world.

In its first form a central drum about 22 m high and 22 m wide, lit by 22 windows, rose over three rings of walkways, the outer one 66 m across, with four chapels reaching out in the shape of a Greek cross. Popes added mosaics and coloured marble in the 6th century; a 7th-century mosaic of two martyrs on each side of a jewelled cross survives in one chapel. In 1139 to 1143 Pope Innocent II gave up the outer ring and three of the chapels, built arches across the middle to hold up the roof, and walled up most of the windows, leaving the smaller church seen today. By the mid 15th century it stood roofless, and Bernardo Rossellino restored it in the 1450s, probably guided by Leon Battista Alberti.

Pope Nicholas V gave it in 1454 to the Pauline Fathers, the only Catholic order founded by Hungarians, and it became Hungary's church in Rome, honouring also King Stephen I of Hungary. For Pope Gregory XIII in the 16th century, Niccolò Circignani and Antonio Tempesta painted the walls with 34 scenes of martyrdom, each with the name of the emperor who ordered it. Under the church lie the barracks of soldiers on special service to the capital and their 2nd-century shrine of Mithras, still being excavated.
